findings.title: Rendering renamed auxiliary XML parts can exhaust the process stack
findings.summary: A document author can point internal numbering, fontTable, theme, styles or settings relationships at deeply nested XML under non-XML filenames. Admission skips XML policy on those auxiliary filenames, but the concrete renderer consumers parse them recursively, allowing a compact DOCX to terminate conversion.

severity.rationale: Attacker-controlled document data deterministically bypasses the depth policy and can abort a local conversion or an embedding worker. Exposure is constrained to a caller choosing to process that document; no remote service or cross-tenant deployment is established, and SECURITY.md recommends process CPU/memory limits.
severity.changeConditions: A shared service accepting public document uploads without per-job process isolation would increase operational impact; enforcing XML limits at each semantic consumer removes this path.

confidence.rationale: Static trace connects the extension-based admission decision, relationship-selected numbering part and unchecked recursive parser. No runtime trigger was executed.

codeEvidence.label: Render entry admits package
codeEvidence.explanation: Caller-controlled DOCX bytes are admitted before the same bytes are normalized and opened.

codeEvidence.label: Admission chooses XML by extension
codeEvidence.explanation: Only .xml and .rels entries receive XML policy checks; a numbering.bin entry is treated as binary.

codeEvidence.label: Only the main part has an extension exception
codeEvidence.explanation: The extra check for non-XML names applies to the main document, leaving auxiliary relationship targets unchecked.

codeEvidence.label: Numbering relationship controls the selected part
codeEvidence.explanation: The document's internal numbering relationship selects an arbitrary package part, excluding external targets but imposing no XML policy.

codeEvidence.label: Selected numbering bytes reach permissive parsing
codeEvidence.explanation: The selected part is decoded as text and passed to the recursive DOM parser without checked parsing.

codeEvidence.label: DOM recursion has no depth argument
codeEvidence.explanation: Each nested element recursively invokes parse_element; the skipped admission depth bound is the only protection on this path.

codeEvidence.label: Layout loads font metadata
codeEvidence.code:
let table = font_table::load_font_table(&pkg);
    let mut embedded = font_table::load_embedded_fonts(&pkg, &table);
codeEvidence.explanation: Layout unconditionally loads font-table metadata before document rendering.

codeEvidence.label: Font-table XML bypasses checked parsing
codeEvidence.explanation: The internal fontTable relationship selects bytes by any filename; parse_font_table_xml builds a DOM without a policy gate.

codeEvidence.label: Theme relationship bytes are parsed unchecked
codeEvidence.explanation: A theme relationship can select a non-.xml part and pass it to the same unchecked recursive DOM parser.

codeEvidence.label: Style relationship bytes are parsed unchecked
codeEvidence.explanation: The selected style part reaches parse_xdocument after optional style transformation, without validating XML depth.

codeEvidence.label: Settings follows the selected part
codeEvidence.explanation: Settings bytes selected by settings_part are forwarded to settings_dom_xml regardless of extension.

codeEvidence.label: Settings cache miss parses unchecked
codeEvidence.explanation: On first use the selected settings bytes reach recursive DOM construction with no independent depth check.

rootCause.summary: `admit()` classifies XML by filename and only adds a nonstandard-extension exception for the main part. `main_rel_part()` trusts internal relationship targets, so `load_numbering()` can select an auxiliary `.bin` part. `parse_numbering_xml()` invokes the permissive DOM parser, whose element recursion has no depth limit, without validating the selected bytes. Independently checked fontTable, theme, styles and settings consumers repeat this relationship-to-unchecked-parser path; the same extension-based admission control fails for each.

findings.remediation: Apply the active XML depth/tag limits to every relationship-selected part immediately before DOM parsing, regardless of filename, and use bounded or iterative parsing as defense in depth.

limitations: No malicious file was generated or executed.
Other auxiliary XML consumers have not been exhaustively enumerated.
validation.summary: Verified that `with_layout()` admits input, `admit()` omits XML checks on non-.xml/.rels auxiliary entries, `main_rel_part()` selects the attacker-controlled internal target, and `load_numbering()` parses it without a second check. PartFs inflation caps and strict translation constrain bytes but do not validate the auxiliary XML nesting. Parent also verified fontTable/theme/styles/settings concrete consumers and their unchecked DOM calls.

dataflow.summary: DOCX bytes -> admission extension filter -> internal numbering relationship -> part_string -> parse_numbering_xml -> recursive parse_element
dataflow.source: attacker-controlled package relationship and auxiliary part bytes

attackPath.summary: Supply a valid DOCX whose numbering relationship targets a `.bin` entry containing deeply nested elements, then call `docx_to_pdf()` or another renderer using the shared layout pipeline.

originalFinding.title: Related XML parts with non-XML extensions bypass depth admission and reach recursive parsing
originalFinding.attacker: An attacker supplying a DOCX for PDF/PNG rendering.
originalFinding.violated_security_invariant: Every untrusted XML part must satisfy the configured XML depth limit before recursive DOM construction.
originalFinding.source_to_sink: Admission checks XML depth only for names ending in .xml or .rels, with an additional exception solely for the main document. The renderer resolves the numbering relationship to an arbitrary internal target, loads that target as XML regardless of extension, and passes it directly to the recursive permissive parser.
originalFinding.impact: A small DOCX containing a numbering relationship targeting numbering.bin with sufficiently deep nested elements can exhaust the native process stack or trap its WASM instance. Native Python consumers can lose their entire hosting process.
supporting_source_evidence: Admission sets is_xml = lower.ends_with(".xml") || lower.ends_with(".rels"); other entries are drained without check_xml_depth.
main_rel_part resolves an internal relationship target without requiring an XML filename.
load_numbering calls parse_numbering_xml on the resolved part; parse_numbering_xml calls dom.parse_xdocument(xml).
Parser::parse_element recursively invokes self.parse_element(scope) for child elements without a local depth check.
counterevidence: ZIP compressed/inflated byte limits remain effective, but deeply nested XML requires little input space.
Admission separately checks a main part with an unusual extension; that exception does not cover numbering or other auxiliary parts.
Checked inspect parsing validates related XML separately, but rendering uses the unchecked parser.
No application code was executed; the conclusion follows the static call chain.
originalFinding.remediation: Apply XML policy to every part consumed as XML regardless of its filename, preferably at a common checked part-loading boundary. Enforce depth during DOM construction as defense in depth.

originalCandidate.originalEvidence: load_font_table follows fontTable relationship to arbitrary part extension (font_table_part -> main_rel_part), then part_string -> parse_font_table_xml -> infallible recursive DOM parse (font_table.rs:66-78). Admission scans XML by .xml/.rels extension except main document, so a fontTable relationship targeting word/faces.bin can carry arbitrarily deep XML under byte limits without max_xml_depth validation. Existing test follows a renamed .xml part but no extension constraint.
originalCandidate.siblingEvidence: Confirmed broader extension bypass: theme main_rel_part -> parse_theme_xml (src/convert/mod.rs:3305-3317), styles (3480-3497), numbering (6557-6569), settings (6866-6888), and fontTable (src/convert/font_table.rs:66-78) all parse relationship-selected non-.xml bytes with unchecked DOM parser. PartFs::read_package only checks byte/resource totals and OPC metadata attributes (src/opc/mod.rs:282-385), not auxiliary XML depth.

findings.title: Importing a cyclic drawing payload can terminate Markdown conversion
findings.summary: A Markdown author can supply a `drawing:` image payload with a dependency that points to itself. JSON decoding accepts that graph and package assembly recursively materializes it without tracking visited dependencies, exhausting the conversion process stack.

severity.rationale: A small attacker-supplied Markdown image payload can abort a caller processing it, including native or WASM conversion. This is a constrained document-processing availability failure; remote multi-user deployment is not established and process quotas are a caller obligation.
severity.changeConditions: A shared unisolated Markdown conversion service would increase impact; rejecting cycles or memoizing in-progress parts removes the deterministic trigger.

confidence.rationale: Independent source trace verifies direct public Markdown acceptance, unvalidated dependency indices, and recursive traversal with no cycle guard; no application code was executed.

rootCause.summary: `picture()` accepts a decoded `Drawing` from caller-controlled Markdown and package assembly invokes `materialize()`. Root relationships select dependency indices. `dep_part()` inserts a generated filename into `used`, but does not mark the dependency index as in progress or completed before following its relationships. A self-edge therefore re-enters the same dependency indefinitely; filename collision handling does not stop the graph recursion.

findings.remediation: Validate and bound the drawing dependency graph before assembly; use a per-index in-progress/completed map to reject cycles or allocate each output part once before resolving links.

limitations: No crafted input was generated or executed.
A valid captured graph cycle may also reproduce this, but the proven path is author-supplied Markdown.
validation.summary: Verified a single dependency with `rels[].part` pointing to its own valid index passes the only index checks. `dep_part()` recursively invokes itself before writing/comparing the part bytes. findings.title: Converting a small legacy DOC can allocate gigabytes through reused text pieces
findings.summary: A legacy DOC can reuse the same physical text range across many logical pieces. Conversion expands every declared character into a `StoryChar` without a decoded-output budget, so a roughly megabyte-sized input can exhaust host memory before DOCX admission.

severity.rationale: A hostile legacy document can exhaust a local or embedding process using strong input amplification. The victim must choose to convert the input; no public service or tenant crossing is established and process memory limits constrain the operational scope.
severity.changeConditions: Evidence of a shared service accepting untrusted input without job isolation, or broader cross-user exposure, would raise impact; enforcing the stated invariant or removing the required shared-directory condition would reduce it.

confidence.rationale: Independent static source review establishes attacker input, control failure and sink; no runtime reproduction or application execution was performed.

codeEvidence.explanation: Each attacker-selected PCD supplies an independent physical offset; repeated offsets are not rejected and can back many logical ranges.

codeEvidence.explanation: The check requires logical CP coverage but puts no practical bound on ccp_text or cumulative output records before allocating the Vec.

codeEvidence.label: Loop follows logical CP ranges
codeEvidence.explanation: Every logical CP maps back into the physical range of its piece; repeated ranges remain valid checked reads while expanding the same bytes again.

codeEvidence.label: Each decoded character becomes a record
codeEvidence.explanation: One StoryChar is pushed for every decoded logical character, making memory proportional to attacker-declared logical expansion.

rootCause.summary: `read()` obtains the attacker-controlled FIB character count and piece table. `pieces()` decodes each physical offset independently. `main_text()` checks logical CP order/coverage and each physical byte access, but accepts repeated physical ranges and appends a character record for every logical CP. Neither checked offsets nor a u32 character count supplies a practical decoded-memory budget.

findings.remediation: Add an active legacy-input limit on logical characters and cumulative decoded memory, checked before iterating or allocating; charge repeated physical ranges against the output budget.

limitations: No application code, exploit input or tests were executed.
Live deployment and process isolation are unknown.

Native CLI calls doc_to_docx before its nonlegacy admission branch. No allocation experiment was run.

codeEvidence.label: Each character rescans the full field stack
codeEvidence.explanation: Every character scans all field-state booleans; begin adds one state and separator makes its top false, allowing an arbitrarily long all-false prefix.

validation.summary: Independently inspected the complete field transition loop: for N begin/separator pairs, the stack grows to N while each prior level is false, producing at least the triangular number of checks. findings.title: Rendering a DOCX table can allocate billions of columns from a small integer
findings.summary: A DOCX table can set `gridSpan`, `gridBefore` or `gridAfter` to a huge integer. The renderer treats it as row occupancy and allocates grid-sized vectors without a maximum, exhausting memory despite bounded input bytes and XML depth.

severity.rationale: A document author can reliably trigger local layout memory exhaustion with tiny input. Exposure is limited to processing the selected document; a shared public rendering deployment is not established.
severity.changeConditions: Evidence of a shared service accepting untrusted input without job isolation, or broader cross-user exposure, would raise impact; enforcing the stated invariant or removing the required shared-directory condition would reduce it.

confidence.rationale: Independent static source review establishes attacker input, control failure and sink; no runtime reproduction or application execution was performed.

rootCause.summary: The shared layout entry admits package bytes, then table parsing obtains `gridSpan` through an unrestricted usize conversion and puts it into `RawCell.colspan`. Row `gridBefore`/`gridAfter` values likewise become placeholder-cell spans. `table_block()` sums these spans into occupancy and directly grows `cols` to that length. `stretch_stale_spans()` leaves already oversized occupancy unchanged, so it supplies no cap.

findings.remediation: Enforce an active table-column budget on gridSpan, gridBefore, gridAfter and checked aggregate occupancy before expanding vectors, and carry it through merge/span bookkeeping; use fallible allocation.

limitations: No application code, exploit input or tests were executed.
Live deployment and process isolation are unknown.

Archive/XML budgets and downstream raster DPI/page limits do not constrain this pre-raster layout allocation.

findings.title: Rendering an HTML altChunk can expand a small colspan into gigabytes of XML
findings.summary: An internal HTML or MHT altChunk with a huge `colspan` makes the renderer emit one XML grid-column element per numeric column. A tiny package can consume gigabytes while generating XML before normal layout begins.

severity.rationale: A document author can trigger strong memory/CPU amplification in a chosen conversion. No public shared-service deployment is established; process-level limits constrain the damage to the job.

codeEvidence.explanation: After admission, main-document altChunk relationship bytes are loaded from the package and expanded before unchecked DOM parsing.

codeEvidence.label: Chunk bytes become generated WML
codeEvidence.explanation: The selected internal bytes are decoded as HTML/MHT and passed to html_to_wml, preserving attacker control of table attributes.

let cols = table
            .rows

            .map(|r| r.iter().map(|c| c.span).sum::<usize>())
            .max()

codeEvidence.label: Each column appends another XML element
codeEvidence.explanation: Emission iterates once per numeric column, appending XML without an output budget before the later table layout code can run.

rootCause.summary: `with_layout()` admits the original package and then replaces altChunks with generated WML. `expand()` reads package chunk bytes and calls `html_to_wml()`. This exhausts resources before the distinct DOCX grid allocator.

findings.remediation: Bound individual HTML colspan and aggregate columns with checked arithmetic and enforce a generated-WML byte budget while emitting HTML/MHT altChunks.

limitations: No application code, exploit input or tests were executed.
Live deployment and process isolation are unknown.
validation.summary: Independently verified that internal bytes are loaded into the HTML converter, colspan receives only parse/default/max(1), and each numeric column causes additional string output. Admission bounds original HTML bytes, not expanded WML; later image/raster limits cannot constrain this earlier string construction.

findings.title: Recording an edit plan can overwrite another user's file through a predictable staging symlink
findings.summary: Python and Node plan-recording CLIs write to a predictable basename-and-PID `.partial` path using ordinary truncating writes. A local attacker who can create entries in the victim's plan directory can plant a symlink there and make the plan JSON overwrite another victim-writable file.

severity.rationale: The write crosses a real filesystem privilege boundary but requires a shared writable directory, prediction/knowledge of a victim PID, a successful plan and permissive link-follow behavior. Protected or private plan directories mitigate it. Those constrained prerequisites support low severity.
severity.changeConditions: Evidence of a shared service accepting untrusted input without job isolation, or broader cross-user exposure, would raise impact; enforcing the stated invariant or removing the required shared-directory condition would reduce it.

confidence.rationale: Independent static source review establishes attacker input, control failure and sink; no runtime reproduction or application execution was performed.

codeEvidence.label: Python previews before writing
codeEvidence.explanation: Python requires a successful plan preview before proceeding, constraining reachability but not securing the subsequent staging path.

codeEvidence.label: Python uses predictable nonexclusive staging
codeEvidence.explanation: Python computes a basename/PID sibling path and uses Path.write_bytes before replacement; a preexisting symlink can redirect that truncating write.

codeEvidence.label: Node previews before writing
codeEvidence.explanation: Node similarly gates recording on successful validation and preview before touching the separate staging path.

codeEvidence.label: Node uses predictable nonexclusive staging
codeEvidence.explanation: Node computes the same predictable sibling pattern and uses fs.writeFileSync without exclusive creation; rename follows the already redirected write.

rootCause.summary: Both wrappers validate and preview the proposed plan, then resolve the final plan path. They derive a sibling temporary pathname from its basename and the process PID, without exclusive creation or a private directory. Python Path.write_bytes and Node fs.writeFileSync follow a preexisting symlink and truncate its referent. Subsequent atomic replacement of the plan cannot undo that earlier unauthorized write. Secure native publication is not called by either wrapper.

findings.remediation: Create staging storage exclusively using a secure temporary-file API or private random directory, write through its returned handle, and atomically replace the intended destination; refuse preexisting staging links.

limitations: No application code, exploit input or tests were executed.
Live deployment and process isolation are unknown.
validation.summary: Verified both wrapper functions and their success/preview gates. Neither uses an exclusive/no-follow open or securely created private staging directory. A preexisting symlink in a shared writable non-sticky directory can therefore redirect the initial staging write; resolving the final plan target does not validate that separate temporary path. Requires victim-writable referent and OS permission to follow the link. No filesystem writes were performed.

originalFinding.title: Predictable plan staging filenames permit symlink-based arbitrary file truncation
originalFinding.attacker: A local attacker able to create files in a directory where another user records an edit plan.
originalFinding.violated_security_invariant: Recording a plan must only modify its authorized destination and securely created staging storage.
originalFinding.source_to_sink: Both hosted CLIs derive their temporary filename solely from the target basename and process PID, then write to it using ordinary truncating file writes. An attacker can precreate that predictable .partial pathname as a symlink to a file writable by the victim. The staging write follows the link and overwrites the referent before the subsequent rename.
originalFinding.impact: When the victim records operations with edit/add --plan in a shared writable directory, the attacker can clobber a different victim-writable file with the generated plan JSON. This can corrupt configuration or other sensitive files outside the requested plan destination.
supporting_source_evidence: Python constructs partial = target.with_name(f".{target.name}.{os.getpid()}.partial") and calls partial.write_bytes before os.replace.
Node constructs `.${path.basename(target)}.${process.pid}.partial` and calls fs.writeFileSync before fs.renameSync.
Neither path uses exclusive creation, a no-follow open, unpredictable secure temporary storage, or the native publication staging API.
counterevidence: The attacker needs local directory-write access and knowledge or prediction of the victim process PID.
Plan preview must succeed before the vulnerable write.
Resolving the final plan target does not secure the subsequently constructed temporary pathname.
The native publication implementation uses private staging, but these two plan-recording paths do not invoke it.
No files were modified and no exploit was executed.
originalFinding.remediation: Create staging files exclusively using a secure temporary-file API or a private randomly named staging directory, write through the returned handle, and atomically rename the securely created file. Refuse preexisting staging paths and symlinks.

threatModel.summary: Jubarte processes untrusted DOCX/OOXML, Markdown, and legacy DOC into document views, edited packages, tracked-change redlines, PDF/PNG, and reports. The Rust engine is consumed by its native CLI, PyO3 Python APIs/CLI, and wasm-bindgen browser/Node APIs and Node CLI. Python additionally provides a stdio MCP server with explicit directory-capability document/artifact I/O. Native rendering also performs ambient font discovery and font-index persistence, so the engine is not universally filesystem-pure. The optional native self-update command downloads a GitHub release and replaces the executable; release automation separately holds publication/signing authority. Sources: src/lib.rs:7-35, src/lib.rs:163-165, Cargo.toml:82-99, jubarte-python/Cargo.toml:31-39, jubarte-wasm/Cargo.toml:14-32, jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:67-108, jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:373-381, src/convert/font.rs:3090-3107, src/convert/font.rs:3213-3229, src/update.rs:186-257, .github/workflows/release.yml:230-265.
assets: Confidential document content, embedded media, revisions, comments, authors, metadata, rendered output, and edit reports entrusted to the processing host and intentionally returned or exported by its selected interface. Integrity of document edits and correspondence between a plan and its intended input snapshot. The legacy edit path verifies source_sha256 when provided; this guard is optional and recorded as guarded in its report. Sources: src/edit.rs:2081-2088, src/edit.rs:2480-2482.

Filesystem authority granted to MCP: canonical root and paths beneath it, including out_dir/clean.docx, redline.docx, patch.diff, report.json, optional redline.pdf and redline-page-NN.png; render exports use out_dir/page-NN.png and render.pdf. Sources: jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:69-108,185-217,234-255.
